paragraphs: Our Sages of blessed memory said that a Jew who has a legal dispute with a gentile should try to evade it (postpone the proceeding) until Rosh Chodesh Elul, and some say only until Tisha B'Av, meaning until after the tenth of Av -- and this latter view is the main one, that there is no need to evade it until Rosh Chodesh Elul but only until after the tenth of Av, especially since on the fifteenth of Av one must make rejoicing, because there is an elevation for the Shechinah, as is written in the holy Zohar, part 2, page 195; and since this month rose up on the fifteenth day, it does not go back down, for one ascends in holiness [and does not descend]. And with this I have explained, with the help of Heaven, the hint in the verse: "Joseph is a fruitful son, a fruitful son by a spring (or: by the eye); the daughters walked upon the wall" (Bereishit 49:22) -- for it is known that our Sages of blessed memory said there were no [greater] festive days for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur, on which the daughters of Israel would go out and dance in the vineyards, as mentioned in tractate Ta'anit, see there. And it is known that our Sages of blessed memory said in the Midrash that all of Israel are called by the name "Joseph," as it is written, "Be gracious to the remnant of Joseph." And this is what it means: "Joseph is a fruitful son" -- these are Israel, who will have a "fruitful son by the eye," which is the month of Av, which is the aspect of "eye" as mentioned above, even though it contains weeping and mourning. And it says: when will this favor come? In the month of Av, which is the aspect of "eye," and it says, "the daughters walked upon [shur]," meaning: at the time when the daughters of Israel go out and dance in the vineyards, which is on the fifteenth of Av.

clarification.explanation: A Jew who has a lawsuit with a gentile should try to postpone and delay it until after the tenth of Av only (and need not wait until Rosh Chodesh Elul, per the stricter opinion), because the mazal of the month of Av is weak at its beginning. But from the fifteenth of Av onward there is elevation and joy, since "one ascends in holiness," and as our Sages said, there were no [greater] festive days for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur, on which the daughters of Israel would go out and dance in the vineyards. With this the Ben Ish Chai interprets, by way of secret meaning, the verse "Joseph is a fruitful son, a fruitful son by the eye; the daughters walked upon the wall": since all of Israel are called by the name "Joseph" (as it is written, "Be gracious to the remnant of Joseph"), "Joseph is a fruitful son" refers to Israel, who are destined to have "a fruitful [son] by the eye" -- favor and blessing in the month of Av, which is in the aspect of "eye" (as explained in the introduction to the parasha), even though it contains weeping and mourning. And when will this favor come? "The daughters walked upon [shur]" -- at the time when the daughters of Israel go out and dance in the vineyards, namely on the fifteenth of Av.
takeaways: A lawsuit with a gentile -- it is preferable to postpone it until after the tenth of Av (due to the weakness of the mazal at the start of Av).
The fifteenth of Av -- a day of joy and elevation (one ascends in holiness), like Yom Kippur.

By secret meaning: "Joseph is a fruitful son... the daughters walked upon [shur]" is expounded upon Israel (called by the name Joseph), who merit favor in the month of Av (the aspect of "eye") specifically on the fifteenth day of it.

paragraphs: That which they said, that one should minimize business dealings from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av, refers specifically to dealings connected with joy, such as wedding preparations; but other ordinary commerce and the like is conducted as usual, without concern. And even wedding preparations -- if one wants to buy something he will not be able to buy after Tisha B'Av, or something for which there will not be time to make after Tisha B'Av, it is permitted; and the same law applies to something he could buy after Tisha B'Av, but he now finds it at a bargain price such that he could not buy it at this rate afterward -- it is permitted to buy it before Tisha B'Av.

clarification.explanation: What they said about minimizing business dealings from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av applies specifically to dealings connected with joy (such as wedding preparations), but other ordinary commerce is conducted as usual. And even wedding preparations -- if they cannot be bought after Tisha B'Av, or there will be no time to prepare them afterward, or they are now found at a bargain that will not be available later -- it is permitted to buy them before Tisha B'Av.
takeaways: The minimizing of business dealings applies only to matters of joy; ordinary commerce continues as usual.
Wedding preparations that cannot or should not be postponed -- permitted to buy before Tisha B'Av.

paragraphs: If construction is not an essential matter, one should not begin it from Rosh Chodesh [Av]; but if he began before, one does not stop. And if it is an essential matter where there is concern of loss, and certainly of danger, it is permitted to begin even from Rosh Chodesh; and likewise a safety railing (ma'akeh) may be started even after Rosh Chodesh. But decorative painting and carving (tziyur v'chiyur) -- even if begun beforehand -- is forbidden to be done from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av, and even where contracted out it is good to be careful; and if he has already made the contract, if he can appease the contractor with a small amount to wait until after Tisha B'Av, that is proper, and if not, it is permitted. And the prohibition on tziyur v'chiyur applies both to decorative work done in construction and to that done in wood by carpenters' craft; and even other construction that is not tziyur v'chiyur, if the construction is for spaciousness/comfort, its law is like tziyur v'chiyur, that even if he began it before Rosh Chodesh [he must stop]. However, in a synagogue one may build even on the eve of Tisha B'Av, and even tziyur v'chiyur, since it is for the sake of a mitzvah.

clarification.explanation: Non-essential construction should not be started from Rosh Chodesh, but if it was started earlier, one does not stop; and essential construction (where there is concern of loss, and certainly of danger) -- it is permitted to start even from Rosh Chodesh, and likewise a safety railing. But decorative painting and carving (ornamental work) are forbidden from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av even if begun beforehand, and one should also be careful with contract work -- and one who has already closed a contract, if he can appease the contractor with a small amount to wait until after Tisha B'Av, that is proper; and if not, it is permitted. The prohibition on decorative work includes woodwork in carpentry as well; and construction for spaciousness/comfort has the same law as decorative work. In a synagogue it is permitted to build even on the eve of Tisha B'Av (a mitzvah need).
takeaways: Non-essential construction -- not begun from Rosh Chodesh (essential construction or a safety railing -- permitted).
Ornamental work (decorative painting/carving, comfort construction) -- forbidden; a synagogue -- permitted.

paragraphs: Even though according to the strict law weddings are forbidden only from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av, nevertheless the custom is to forbid them from the seventeenth of Tammuz; but betrothals (eirusin) and matchmaking (shidduchin) are permitted. And here in our city of Baghdad, may it be guarded, the custom is to make betrothals after the seventeenth of Tammuz, but from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av one does not make betrothals or matchmaking arrangements. See Shiyurei Kenesset HaGedolah 551, glosses on the Tur, letter heh, that some have the custom not to make betrothals from the seventeenth of Tammuz, and it is proper to follow this practice.

clarification.explanation: Even though by strict law weddings are forbidden only from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av, the custom is to forbid them from the seventeenth of Tammuz; but betrothals and matchmaking are permitted. The custom in Baghdad is to make betrothals after the seventeenth of Tammuz, but from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av one does not make even betrothals or matchmaking arrangements.
takeaways: Weddings -- the custom is to forbid them from the seventeenth of Tammuz.
Betrothals and matchmaking are permitted, but not from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av (Baghdad custom).

paragraphs: It is forbidden to dance and hold festive dances from the seventeenth of Tammuz until after Tisha B'Av. And it is proper to warn Jewish musicians not to sing/play for gentiles; but on account of ill will (eivah), or if the musician has nothing to eat, it is permitted to play for gentiles for his wage. All this applies after the seventeenth of Tammuz, but from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av they should refrain entirely; and the same law applies on the seventeenth of Tammuz itself -- he should not go under any circumstance, and those who go for their wage do not see a sign of blessing. And likewise one must be careful on the tenth of Tevet, at night and during the day, not to dance or hold festive dances. See Eliyah Rabbah, small section 1, and Eshel Avraham, end of small section 10, and other later authorities.

clarification.explanation: Dancing and festive dances are forbidden from the seventeenth of Tammuz until after Tisha B'Av. It is proper to warn Jewish musicians not to play for gentiles; but on account of ill will, or if the musician has nothing to eat, it is permitted to play for his wage. All this applies after the seventeenth of Tammuz, but from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av they should refrain entirely, and even on the seventeenth of Tammuz itself he should not go at all (and those who go for their wage do not see a sign of blessing). And one must likewise be careful on the tenth of Tevet.
takeaways: Dancing and festive dances are forbidden from the seventeenth of Tammuz until after Tisha B'Av.
A musician should refrain from playing for gentiles (and from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av, entirely), except due to ill will or livelihood.

paragraphs: In the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, it is forbidden by strict law to launder, even if one does not wish to wear the item now but only to set it aside until after Tisha B'Av; and even if he has only a single shirt, it is forbidden. And likewise garments laundered beforehand are forbidden, both to wear and to make up the bed with them. And in places where there is great heat at this time, so that people sweat greatly and are forced to change their shirt, particularly women -- what should one do? He should wear, before Shabbat, the laundered shirt for the duration of an hour, then remove it and put it away to wear after Shabbat, within this week in which Tisha B'Av falls. But if he forgot to make this arrangement before Shabbat and remembered on the day of Shabbat itself, he should not do so -- wearing the laundered shirt for an hour and removing it to wear after Shabbat -- for if he did so, he would be found preparing on Shabbat for the sake of the weekday, [which is forbidden]. What should he do instead? He should remove the shirt he is wearing, which he put on Friday night, and put on the laundered one in its place, and it should remain on him, and he should not remove it that day; and then that shirt which he removed on the day of Shabbat he shall wear after Shabbat, since it has not yet become sweaty and soiled, as it was not worn for very long -- so I have concluded in my holy work Makbetziel. And so he shall do with socks and other garments needed during this week. And it is forbidden to launder during this week even hand-towels and table-napkins, and only a handkerchief used for wiping the nose is permitted to be laundered. And socks are forbidden to be laundered, and it is forbidden to wear laundered ones -- see Beit David, siman 332. And even for young children who have not yet reached the age of chinuch (training in mitzvot) it is forbidden to launder [their clothes]; but garments in which small children are wrapped, who pass stool and urinate in them, are permitted to be laundered. And some have the custom of permitting the laundering of clothes of children up to three years of age, and one should not protest against them; only one must warn them not to launder many together, and to launder discreetly. And it is forbidden for a Jewish woman to launder in her house for a gentile, on account of the appearance of impropriety, since people will think it belongs to a Jew; but if it is recognizable that the items belong to a gentile, it is permitted. And there is room to be lenient to launder in her house discreetly even when it is not recognizable that they belong to a gentile.

clarification.explanation: In the week in which Tisha B'Av falls it is forbidden by strict law to launder, even in order to put the item away for after the fast, and even if he has only a single shirt; and garments laundered beforehand are forbidden to wear or to make up the bed with. In a place of heat where people sweat and are forced to change their shirt: he should wear a laundered shirt before Shabbat for the duration of an hour, remove it, and set it aside for the weekdays of that week. If he forgot and remembered on Shabbat itself -- he should not do so (as it would be preparing on Shabbat for the weekday); rather, he should remove the shirt he wore Friday night and put on the laundered one in its place, leaving it on, and the one he removed he shall wear after Shabbat. And it is forbidden to launder even hand-towels and table-napkins (a handkerchief for the nose is permitted), and also for children; but infants' diapers are permitted. And some are lenient regarding the laundering of clothes of children up to age three, and one should not protest against them -- provided they do not launder many together, and that they launder discreetly. And it is forbidden for a Jewish woman to launder gentile clothing in her home, on account of the appearance of impropriety, that people would think it belongs to a Jew; but if it is recognizable as belonging to a gentile, it is permitted, and there is room to be lenient to launder discreetly even when it is not recognizable.
takeaways: In the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, laundering and wearing laundered items are forbidden, even to set aside for after the fast.
In hot weather -- the stratagem of "wearing a laundered item for an hour before Shabbat and setting it aside" (and if forgotten -- switch on Shabbat itself and leave it on).
The leniency for children's clothing depends on two conditions: not laundering many together, and laundering discreetly.

paragraphs: Even though laundering during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls is forbidden even by a gentile, nevertheless, if Tisha B'Av falls on a Thursday and it is not possible to launder on Friday, the Gaon Rav Yaavetz (Rabbi Yaakov Emden), of blessed memory, permitted laundering by a gentile, since it is not possible to launder on the eve of Shabbat; but by a Jew it is forbidden. See Machazik Berachah, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: Even though laundering in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls is forbidden even by a gentile, if Tisha B'Av falls on a Thursday and it is not possible to launder on Friday, the Yaavetz permitted laundering by a gentile (since it is not possible to launder on the eve of Shabbat); but by a Jew it is forbidden.
takeaways: Tisha B'Av falling on Thursday -- it is permitted to launder via a gentile for the sake of Shabbat (by a Jew it is forbidden).

paragraphs: In the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, it is forbidden by strict law to wear new clothes, and even new shoes are forbidden to be worn during this week; and from the standpoint of custom, all this is forbidden from Rosh Chodesh.

clarification.explanation: In the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, it is forbidden by strict law to wear new clothes, and even new shoes; and by custom, all this is forbidden already from Rosh Chodesh.
takeaways: New clothes and shoes -- forbidden in the week in which it falls (and by custom, from Rosh Chodesh).

paragraphs: Sewing garments and the like is forbidden during this week, and one should be stringent from Rosh Chodesh. And likewise a Jewish craftsman is forbidden to do this work, whether for pay or for free. And it is written in Machazik Berachah in the name of the Gaon Yaavetz, of blessed memory, that spinning and weaving are also included in this prohibition -- see there. Therefore Jews engaged in the craft of weaving, to weave bobbins (spools of thread), are forbidden to work at it in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls; therefore everyone should warn the members of his household not to sew any garment from Rosh Chodesh until the fast, and not to weave even socks, and not to do embroidery work on garments at all, for all these are actual garments and a complete finishing. And it seems to me that not only is embroidery on something ready to be worn immediately after the embroidery work (such as a belt) forbidden, but even lace embroidery done on pieces of fabric, so that afterward one will make garments from them to wear, which still require cutting and sewing -- that too is forbidden. See our teacher the Rema, of blessed memory, in Darkei Moshe, who wrote that they only permitted the spinning of threads, but the garment itself is forbidden -- see there. And see Magen Avraham, small section 23, [regarding] the reason it is permitted to make what are called collar-folds (kerugin), which are woven on wooden frames, because it is not [yet] a garment -- see there. And see Rav Moed L'Chol Chai, siman 10, letter 18, who wrote: one should warn the wheat-sellers and shoemakers not to make repairs anew, and also every person in his house not to sew anything new and not to make socks (gurapim), etc. -- see there.

However, Jewish craftsmen whose livelihood is from this work of sewing garments, or embroidery work, which they do for others for pay, to whom the garments were given before Rosh Chodesh -- it is permitted for them to work on them from Rosh Chodesh; and only in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls is it forbidden even if they were given before Rosh Chodesh. And if they were not given before Rosh Chodesh, one must be careful not to work on them from Rosh Chodesh, and certainly in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, which is forbidden by strict law. See Magen Avraham, small section 24, and see Matteh Yehudah and Eshel Avraham, small section 25, what is noted from section 7 -- see there. Nevertheless, I do not permit this except in a place where we see that the custom has been to permit it when the garments were brought before Rosh Chodesh, for in that case I say to permit it, as I have written in my holy work Makbetziel, to permit them to work on them from Rosh Chodesh, since their livelihood is from this craft and they do it for others; and only in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls should one prevent them. But in places where the custom of leniency was not established, one must certainly be stringent to warn them in every case, since we Sephardim follow after Maran, of blessed memory, and Maran, of blessed memory, did not distinguish in this, and holds that in every case it is forbidden by strict law in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, and forbidden by way of stringency from Rosh Chodesh, as I have written in my holy work Makbetziel. And if this craftsman has nothing to eat, it seems to me that one should permit him to work even in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, as Rav Beit David, of blessed memory, wrote in siman 320, that there it is only forbidden where it is possible for him to hire himself out to gentiles to work for them -- see there. Therefore it seems that there is room to be lenient here in the case of a worker who has nothing to eat.

clarification.explanation:
Sewing garments and the like is forbidden during this week, and one should be stringent from Rosh Chodesh. A Jewish craftsman is forbidden to do this work -- whether for pay or for free. And Machazik Berachah wrote in the name of the Yaavetz, of blessed memory, that spinning and weaving are also included in the prohibition; therefore Jews engaged in weaving are forbidden in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls. Therefore everyone should warn the members of his household not to sew any garment from Rosh Chodesh until the fast, and not to weave even socks, and not to embroider garments at all -- for all these are actual garments and a complete finishing. And it seems that not only is embroidery of something ready to wear immediately (such as a belt) forbidden, but even lace embroidery on pieces of fabric that will still require cutting and sewing is forbidden. (See the Rema in Darkei Moshe, who wrote that only the spinning of threads was permitted, but the garment itself is forbidden; and see Magen Avraham on the reason it is permitted to make collar-folds woven on wooden frames -- since they are not a garment.)
However, Jewish craftsmen whose livelihood is from this work (sewing or embroidery for others for pay), to whom the garments were given before Rosh Chodesh -- it is permitted for them to work on them from Rosh Chodesh, and only in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls is it forbidden even if given beforehand; and if not given before Rosh Chodesh -- one must be careful not to work on them from Rosh Chodesh, and certainly in the week in which it falls. And nevertheless, this leniency (from Rosh Chodesh) applies only in places where the custom has been to permit it when the garments were brought before Rosh Chodesh; but in a place where this was not the custom -- one must be stringent, since we Sephardim follow after Maran, of blessed memory, who did not distinguish in this. And if the craftsman has nothing to eat -- it is permitted for him to work even in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls (following the view of Beit David).
takeaways: Sewing, weaving, spinning, and embroidery are forbidden in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, and one should be stringent from Rosh Chodesh; this includes lace embroidery on fabric.
A craftsman whose livelihood is from this, who received garments before Rosh Chodesh -- permitted from Rosh Chodesh (where the custom is lenient), but not in the week in which it falls.
A poor person who has nothing to eat -- permitted even in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls.

paragraphs: A torn item, and likewise a garment whose sewing has become permitted [to repair], is permitted to be sewn; and likewise the law is that it is permitted to sew a patch onto a garment. See Moed L'Chol Chai, siman 10, letter 18.

clarification.explanation: A torn item, and likewise a garment whose sewing has become permitted, is permitted to be sewn; and likewise it is permitted to sew a patch onto a garment.
takeaways: Repairing a tear and sewing a patch -- permitted.

paragraphs: To fix the warp threads (shti) in order to weave garments, the custom is to forbid this from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av, because the Even HaShetiyah (Foundation Stone) ceased [to be in use], and "shammah" (its name there) is from the language of shtei (warp), and they supported this with the verse, "for the foundations (hashatot) are destroyed" (Tehillim 11:3). And this is not only forbidden when done for oneself, but even when done for others it is likewise forbidden, on account of the custom, whether for pay or for free, as mentioned in Beit Yosef. Nevertheless, women who spin thread in order to sew garments with it, if their livelihood is from this craft, it is permitted for them to spin even in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, since there is no joy in this craft, and it is not comparable to fixing the warp, which is at the beginning of weaving garments and does have joy [associated with it], as mentioned in Terumat HaDeshen, siman 152, and so wrote the Levush, of blessed memory. And although it appears that they only permitted threads for sewing, but threads needed for the warp -- even the spinning of them is forbidden, as the Turei Zahav wrote in small section 7, nevertheless I wrote in my holy work Makbetziel that those whose livelihood is from this may rely on what Rav Machatzit HaShekel wrote, to be lenient with them; therefore workers in spinning and twisting, called in Arabic "kababat" (spools of thread), and likewise those called in Arabic "fatatil" (wicks/cords), since their livelihood is from this craft, one should not prevent them. And see Machazik Berachah, of blessed memory, what he wrote in the name of Rav Yaavetz, of blessed memory (though the book mentioned is not available to us), and I have written there, with the help of Heaven, that it is permitted to weave loops, called in Arabic "zarur" (loops), and likewise cords called "sagal" (tassels/fringes), and likewise what is called "oyah" (embroidery/lace edging), since all of these are not actual garments or completed items, but are made to adorn garments -- see Magen Avraham small section 23, and Eliyah Rabbah, and Chayei Adam, see there. And all this applies to people whose livelihood is from this craft; but homeowners who do it for themselves, and even for others for pay, whose livelihood is not from this craft, must be careful not to do it from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av. See Rav Olat Shabbat, that even in the case discussed in Terumat HaDeshen, he wrote that in practice it requires further study -- see there.

clarification.explanation: Fixing the warp threads to weave garments -- the custom is to forbid this from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av, in remembrance of the Foundation Stone that was removed ("for the foundations are destroyed"), whether for oneself or for others, for pay or for free. But women who spin thread for sewing, if this is their livelihood, are permitted to spin even in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls (there is no joy in this craft, unlike fixing the warp). And likewise workers in spinning and twisting whose livelihood is from this -- they should not be prevented; and it is permitted to weave loops, tassels, and lace-edgings that are not a complete garment. But homeowners who do it for themselves (or for others for pay) and whose livelihood is not from this -- must be careful not to do it from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av.
takeaways: Fixing the warp for weaving -- forbidden from Rosh Chodesh (in remembrance of the Foundation Stone).
Spinning/twisting for one whose livelihood is from it -- permitted even in the week in which it falls; homeowners -- must be careful from Rosh Chodesh.

paragraphs: Haircutting is forbidden by strict law in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, both of the head and of all bodily hair, and some have the custom to be stringent from the seventeenth of Tammuz. And regarding a beard, whatever hinders eating is permitted [to trim]. And even the father of the newborn son [at a brit] and the sandak (one who holds the baby) are forbidden to cut their hair in this week, and it is forbidden for adults to cut children's hair in this week. And if Tisha B'Av falls on a Sunday, or falls on Shabbat and is postponed [to Sunday], behold Maran, of blessed memory, stated simply that it is permitted in both of the surrounding Shabbatot, whether before the fast or after it. And although he wrote that there is one who says the custom is to forbid the entire preceding week except for Thursday and Friday, we follow the simple ruling of Maran, of blessed memory; therefore it is permitted to launder and cut hair in the preceding week. And so is the custom here in our city to launder in the preceding week, for there is no law of "the week in which Tisha B'Av falls" [in that case]. However, regarding haircutting, it is proper to instruct the people according to the custom of the elders, as the Kol Bo wrote, not to cut hair at all before that Shabbat, so that one enters the day of the fast in a disheveled state; and here in our city we do not sharply rebuke those who are lenient in this. See Moed L'Chol Chai, letter 25.

clarification.explanation: Haircutting is forbidden by strict law in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls (the head and all bodily hair), and some are stringent from the seventeenth of Tammuz; and regarding a beard, whatever hinders eating is permitted. Even the father of the newborn son and the sandak are forbidden to cut their hair in this week, and it is forbidden for adults to cut children's hair. And if Tisha B'Av falls on Sunday or is postponed (falls on Shabbat) -- Maran permits laundering and haircutting in both surrounding Shabbatot; therefore the custom in Baghdad is to launder in the preceding week, but regarding haircutting it is proper to follow the custom of the elders not to cut hair at all before that Shabbat, so as to enter the fast in a disheveled state (and one does not rebuke those who are lenient).
takeaways: Haircutting is forbidden in the week in which it falls (a beard hindering eating is permitted).
Postponed/falling on Sunday -- Maran permits laundering and haircutting in the neighboring weeks, but for haircutting it is proper to be stringent until after the fast.

paragraphs: One should not cut one's fingernails in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, but on the eve of Shabbat Chazon it is permitted to cut the fingernails -- see Moed L'Chol Chai, letter 13. And in my holy work Makbetziel I wrote that if the fingernails extend beyond the flesh, it is permitted to cut them even in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, because there is a great obligation according to the secret [teachings] to cut them, as our teacher [the Arizal], of blessed memory, wrote in Etz Chaim, Sha'ar Partzufei Zachar U'Nekevah, chapter 1, and this is his language: "That which extends from the nail and protrudes beyond the flesh must be cut, for there the external [forces] cling and suckle to the fullest extent; therefore the punishment of one who grows his nails long is very severe" -- end of his language. Therefore, if they extend and protrude, it is permitted to trim them even on the eve of Tisha B'Av. And I further say, without fear, that if one happened to be in the thirty days of mourning [for a relative] such that he was unable to trim them on the eve of Tisha B'Av, and the time for trimming them arrived on the day of Tisha B'Av itself, it is permitted for him to trim them on the day of Tisha B'Av, and he should not wait until after Tisha B'Av, so as not to give dominion to the external [forces] to suckle more, particularly on this day when they have increased strength. See Magen Avraham, siman 551, small section 11, and 554, small section 4, that mourning observed discreetly on Tisha B'Av is lighter than [regular] mourning; see Eshel Avraham -- therefore he should trim them discreetly.

clarification.explanation: One should not cut fingernails in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, but on the eve of Shabbat Chazon it is permitted. And if the fingernails extend and protrude beyond the flesh, it is permitted to cut them even in the week in which it falls (and even on the eve of Tisha B'Av), because there is a great obligation according to the secret [teachings] to cut them (there the external [forces] cling). And likewise in the case of a thirty-day mourning period, where one was unable to trim them beforehand and their time arrived on Tisha B'Av -- it is permitted to trim them discreetly, so as not to give the external [forces] dominion.
takeaways: Cutting fingernails is forbidden in the week in which it falls (permitted on the eve of Shabbat Chazon).
Fingernails protruding beyond the flesh -- permitted to cut even then (an obligation according to the secret [teachings]).

paragraphs: To comb one's head with a comb, without washing, only on dry hair -- some forbid this in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, as mentioned in Shiyurei Kenesset HaGedolah, siman 551, glosses on Beit Yosef, letter 31 -- see there. However, this applies only to a man, but for a woman it is permitted -- see Eliyah Rabbah, Dagul MeRevavah, and Eshel Avraham. And although the Gaon [author of] Eshel Avraham leaned toward being lenient even for a man to comb discreetly, it is proper to be stringent, since he too was uncertain, and we should not abandon the plain ruling of the forbidding authority mentioned by the Mahari Bruna, of blessed memory, whom Kenesset HaGedolah, of blessed memory, cited.

clarification.explanation: Combing the head with a comb on dry hair (without washing) -- some forbid this for a man in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, but for a woman it is permitted. And although some leaned toward being lenient even for a man discreetly, it is proper to be stringent.
takeaways: Combing dry hair in the week in which it falls -- proper to be stringent for a man; for a woman it is permitted.

paragraphs: It is forbidden, by force of custom, to eat meat and drink wine in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, and some have the custom [to forbid this] from Rosh Chodesh, and some from the seventeenth of Tammuz. And here in our city of Baghdad, may it be guarded, the custom is to forbid it from the second night of the month of Av until the night of the tenth, because on the day of Tisha B'Av the town's slaughterers customarily slaughter for the eating of the night of the tenth. Also, the custom here in our city is that even at a brit milah feast, one does not eat meat during these days.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden by force of custom to eat meat and drink wine in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls; some have the custom [to forbid this] from Rosh Chodesh, and some from the seventeenth of Tammuz. In Baghdad the custom is to forbid it from the second night of Av until the night of the tenth (on the day of Tisha B'Av they slaughter for the eating of the night of the tenth), and also at a brit milah feast one does not eat meat during these days.
takeaways: Meat and wine are forbidden by custom (Baghdad: from the second night of Av until the night of the tenth).
Even at a brit milah feast, there is no meat during these days.

paragraphs: The custom is not to wash one's entire body from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av, even in cold water; and one accustomed to immersing every Friday should also immerse on the eve of Shabbat Chazon. And it is likewise permitted to wash one's face, hands, and feet in hot water on the eve of Shabbat Chazon, for one accustomed to doing so every Friday. And any washing done for medical/healing purposes is permitted during these days, even in hot water; therefore a pregnant woman who has entered her ninth month, whose custom is to wash in hot water in order to ease the pain of childbirth, is permitted to wash; and likewise one whom a doctor has instructed to wash in hot water -- washes. And one accustomed to immersing after marital relations continues to immerse as usual, and likewise the sandak is permitted to immerse; and one who experienced a seminal emission is permitted to immerse even on the eve of Tisha B'Av, and only on the day of Tisha B'Av itself is it forbidden to immerse, according to Maran, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: The custom is not to wash one's whole body from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av, even in cold water. One accustomed to immersing every Friday should also immerse on the eve of Shabbat Chazon, and is permitted to wash his face, hands, and feet in hot water on that day. All washing for medical purposes is permitted even in hot water (a pregnant woman in her ninth month, one whom a doctor instructed). One accustomed to immersing after marital relations immerses as usual, and likewise the sandak; and one who had a seminal emission may immerse even on the eve of Tisha B'Av -- only on Tisha B'Av itself is immersion forbidden according to Maran.
takeaways: One does not wash the whole body from Rosh Chodesh (even in cold water); washing for medical purposes is permitted.
One accustomed to immersing on the eve of Shabbat/after marital relations -- immerses; on Tisha B'Av itself it is forbidden.

paragraphs: It is written in the book Yosef Ometz [by] an Ashkenazi [authority]: "In the days of my youth I saw a widespread custom not to buy wood after Rosh Chodesh Av until Tisha B'Av; however, nowadays many are lenient. And it is known that in those days the sages of our city were very strict about this matter, and one who bought wood -- they would take it from him and give it to the poor of the charity fund" -- end, see there. And they give a reason for this matter: because the wood of the [Temple] arrangement [on the altar] was discontinued; and as is written in the Yerushalmi, that women had the custom not to buy wool [thread], because the Foundation Stone was discontinued -- and this is a fine custom. And although one should not forcefully prevent those who are lenient, it is proper for every person to be careful in this, not to buy wood -- whether for building or for kindling -- from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av; but to buy thorny brushwood, which is called "shokh," and the like, for kindling, there is no concern whatsoever in this.

clarification.explanation: Some have the custom not to buy wood from Rosh Chodesh Av until Tisha B'Av (in remembrance of the discontinuation of the wood of the [Temple] arrangement), and the sages of Baghdad were very strict about this. Although one should not forcefully prevent those who are lenient, it is proper for every person to be careful not to buy wood -- for building or for kindling -- from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av; but thorny brushwood for kindling may be bought.
takeaways: It is proper not to buy wood (for building or kindling) from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av.
Thorny brushwood for kindling -- permitted.

paragraphs: On the eve of Tisha B'Av, after midday, one should not study Torah except for matters that are permitted to be studied on Tisha B'Av itself. And if it falls on Shabbat, there are several differing opinions among the later authorities, and one may rely on the lenient view; and so I practice, following the lenient view.

clarification.explanation: On the eve of Tisha B'Av, after midday, one should study only the matters permitted to be studied on Tisha B'Av. And if it falls on Shabbat -- there are differing opinions, and one may rely on the lenient view (and so Rabbi Yosef Chaim practices).
takeaways: On the eve of Tisha B'Av after midday -- one studies only what is permitted on Tisha B'Av itself.
Falling on Shabbat -- one may rely on the lenient view.

paragraphs: At the Se'udah HaMafseket (the meal preceding the fast), it is forbidden to eat two cooked dishes, even of one type -- and even one thick and one soft [of the same type] is likewise considered two cooked dishes. And even something that is eaten raw, such as apples and the like, which were cooked in sugar, is considered a cooked dish; and even if one cooked dates and made them into date-honey, called in Arabic "silan," and even if one cooked and refined and filtered sugar and made it into a beverage called "shira" (syrup), that too is considered a cooked dish, since after its cooking it acquires a different taste and also acquires a new name. And one should not eat a hard-boiled egg and a soft-boiled egg [together], for the later authorities were uncertain whether this is considered two cooked dishes. And if one cooked a single type in two pots, the Ritva permits it, and Rav Chabib, of blessed memory, forbids it in a responsum, as is written in the book Kenesset Yisrael, page 31, side 4. And any cooked dish that is customarily cooked from two types together, such as rice and lentils, called "jashri," and the like, is considered one cooked dish and is permitted; and likewise the law applies to those who cook rice and put chickpeas (chumus) in it, that it is considered one cooked dish, since this is always the custom, and so on for similar cases; but rice that one eats together with fried eggs is considered two cooked dishes and is forbidden.

And one may eat several types of raw fruit, and may likewise eat raw fruit together with the cooked dish; and one may also eat with the cooked dish of rice fermented milk/curd, called in Arabic "laban," or in another language "yogurt," for even though it is customary to heat the milk over the fire before it curdles, this heating does not render it a cooked dish, because its taste, name, and appearance do not change through this heating over the fire -- it merely becomes warm. Therefore this laban, called yogurt, is considered like raw fruit and is permitted to be eaten together with a cooked dish of rice and lentils; nevertheless, it is good to distance oneself from this, in order to minimize one's enjoyments at this meal, as Rav Machazik Berachah, of blessed memory, wrote that it is not proper to eat salad with the cooked dish at this meal.

And cheese, if eaten raw, is like raw fruit; but if the cheese was cooked, it has the law of a cooked dish and is forbidden to be eaten with another cooked dish. And although it is permitted to eat several types of raw fruit, nevertheless it is proper to minimize one's enjoyments at this meal and not to indulge in fruit, eating only the fruit he needs for the sake of the fast, such as the fruit called "riqi" (watermelon), which is very much needed in these countries because of the heat.

clarification.explanation: At the Se'udah HaMafseket it is forbidden to eat two cooked dishes, even of one type (one thick and one soft are considered two). Even something eaten raw (apples) that was cooked in sugar, and likewise date-honey (silan) and sugar syrup (shira), are considered cooked dishes. A dish customarily cooked from two types together (rice and lentils, rice with chickpeas) is considered one dish and permitted, but rice with fried eggs is considered two and forbidden. Raw fruit -- permitted in several types, and also together with the cooked dish, and likewise laban (yogurt) with rice, since its heating does not make it a "cooked dish"; but it is good to minimize one's enjoyments at this meal.
takeaways: At the Se'udah HaMafseket -- only one cooked dish (one thick and one soft of the same type = two).
One type cooked together (rice and lentils) is considered one; raw fruit and laban are permitted, but it is good to minimize.

paragraphs: At the Se'udah HaMafseket, one should not sit upon cushions, but rather upon a mat or a thin cloth, and should not sit directly on the ground itself, for this is difficult according to the secret [teachings]; and it is permitted to sit on a plank that is not higher than a handbreadth -- see Moed L'Chol Chai, letter 35. And three people should not sit together to eat at this meal, so that they do not become obligated in zimun (the invitation to Grace After Meals recited by a quorum of three); and the reason, it seems to me, is that zimun indicates permanence/fixedness, and we do not want there to be fixedness for this meal, which is for the mourner, for it is [our hope and] certainty that the Redeemer will come and rebuild the Temple speedily in our days, Amen, and it will become a meal of joy and gladness.

And all the matters mentioned, both regarding the eating of two cooked dishes and regarding the manner of sitting, were said only concerning the Se'udah HaMafseket, after which one does not eat a fixed meal, and also that he eats it after midday; but if his intention is to eat a fixed meal after it, or if he eats it before midday, he need not be careful about any of the above.

clarification.explanation: At the Se'udah HaMafseket one should not sit on cushions but on a mat or thin cloth, and not directly on the ground (difficult according to the secret [teachings]); it is permitted to sit on a plank not higher than a handbreadth. And three should not sit together, so as not to become obligated in zimun -- since we do not want fixedness for this meal of mourning (in the hope that the Redeemer will come and rebuild the Temple, and it will become a meal of joy). All these laws (two cooked dishes and the manner of sitting) apply only to a Se'udah HaMafseket after which one does not eat a fixed meal, and which is eaten after midday; but if he intends to eat a fixed meal afterward, or eats it before midday, he need not be careful about any of this.
takeaways: At the Se'udah HaMafseket one sits low (not on cushions and not on the ground), and does not form a zimun (not three together).
These laws apply only to a Se'udah HaMafseket after midday, after which no fixed meal follows.

paragraphs: One should not walk entirely barefoot on Tisha B'Av; rather, one should wear a cloth shoe, but a leather shoe is forbidden. And if one touched this [cloth] shoe with his hands, he must wash his hands [before touching food, etc.], according to the law of one who touches a leather shoe.

clarification.explanation: One should not walk entirely barefoot on Tisha B'Av, but should wear a cloth shoe; a leather shoe is forbidden. And if one touched this cloth shoe with his hands, he must wash his hands, according to the law of one who touches a leather shoe.
takeaways: On Tisha B'Av one wears a cloth shoe (leather is forbidden).
One who touched the cloth shoe worn on Tisha B'Av must wash his hands, as in the law of touching a leather shoe.

paragraphs: On Tisha B'Av one should not wash, and even to dip one's finger in water is forbidden. And for the hand-washing of the morning or after using the bathroom, one should wash up to the end of the finger-joints. And if there was dirt on his hands or face, it is permitted to wash it off; and likewise one whose eyes customarily tear, and in the morning after he awakens from his sleep there is dirt on his eyelashes -- it is permitted to wash it. And likewise one who has an eye ailment and customarily washes them in cold water for medical treatment -- it is permitted. And likewise those [women] who cook rinse the meat and vegetables in water as usual, without concern.

clarification.explanation: On Tisha B'Av it is forbidden to wash, even to dip a finger in water. For the morning hand-washing or after using the bathroom -- one washes up to the end of the finger-joints. If there was dirt on his hands or face -- it is permitted to wash it off; and likewise one whose eyes tear and there is dirt on his eyelashes in the morning -- permitted to wash it, and likewise one with an eye ailment who washes for medical treatment. And women cooking rinse meat and vegetables as usual.
takeaways: One does not wash on Tisha B'Av (morning hand-washing -- only up to the finger-joints).
Washing off dirt, medical treatment, or cooking needs -- permitted.

paragraphs: Marital relations are forbidden on Tisha B'Av, and therefore it is forbidden to sleep in the same bed as one's wife; and it is proper that he not touch her at night, nor hand her something directly from his hand to hers, on account of [the principle] "Say to the nazirite: go around, go around [and do not approach the vineyard]" [i.e., distance oneself from anything close to the forbidden]. And one does not recite the blessing "who has provided me with all my needs" (she'asah li kol tzorki) on Tisha B'Av, because [in a sense] everyone is barefoot [lacking], as our teacher the Arizal, of blessed memory, wrote. And on the night of Tisha B'Av, one should place a stone beneath the pillow on which he rests his head; and one who is accustomed to sleeping on two [pillows] should change his custom and lie on one.

clarification.explanation: Marital relations are forbidden on Tisha B'Av, and therefore it is forbidden to sleep in the same bed as one's wife; and it is proper that he not touch her at night and not hand her anything directly from his hand ("Say to the nazirite: go around"). And one does not recite the blessing "who has provided me with all my needs" on Tisha B'Av (since, in a sense, everyone is barefoot). On the night of Tisha B'Av one places a stone beneath the pillow on which he rests his head, and one accustomed to sleeping on two pillows changes his custom and sleeps on one.
takeaways: Marital relations are forbidden; one does not sleep in the same bed as one's wife, and is careful to avoid touching her.
One does not recite "who has provided me with all my needs"; and one changes his sleeping custom (a stone beneath the pillow).

paragraphs: There is no greeting of "Shalom" on Tisha B'Av, and likewise it is forbidden to send a gift to one another, whether food or clothing, as mentioned in the Magen Avraham and several other sources. However, to a poor person who is in need, it is permitted to send him [a gift], for this is [an act of] tzedakah, as mentioned in Ruach Chaim. And work is forbidden both at night and during the day; and as for milking the animals, if possible through a gentile, one should do so, and if not, he should milk them himself.

clarification.explanation: There is no greeting of "Shalom" on Tisha B'Av, and likewise it is forbidden to send gifts to one another (whether food or clothing); but to a poor person in need, it is permitted (as an act of charity). Work is forbidden both night and day; and milking -- if possible via a gentile, he should do so, and if not, he milks himself.
takeaways: There is no greeting of "Shalom" and no sending of gifts on Tisha B'Av (to a poor person in need -- permitted, as charity).
Work is forbidden day and night (milking -- preferably by a gentile).

paragraphs: On the day of Tisha B'Av, one puts on tzitzit and tefillin -- both Rashi's and Rabbeinu Tam's -- in the morning at home, and recites the Shema alone; and afterward he goes to the synagogue to pray with the congregation. And those who are accustomed to do this [putting on tefillin] only at the time of Minchah do not act properly. As for the Torah readings "Kadesh" and "V'hayah ki y'vi'akha," some have the custom to say them on Tisha B'Av and some do not say them, and each person should follow his own custom in this. Also, on the night of Tisha B'Av, after midnight, one recites Tikkun Rachel alone; but during the day one does not recite Tikkun Rachel, even though the custom is to recite it every day after midday from the seventeenth of Tammuz onward; and likewise on the day of the eve of Tisha B'Av, one recites it during the day after midday. See Yosef Ometz, siman 25.

clarification.explanation: On the day of Tisha B'Av one puts on tzitzit and tefillin (both Rashi's and Rabbeinu Tam's) in the morning at home and recites only the Shema, and afterward goes to the synagogue to pray with the congregation; and those who delay putting them on until the time of Minchah do not act properly. The Torah readings "Kadesh" and "V'hayah ki y'vi'akha" -- some say them and some do not, each according to his custom. On the night of Tisha B'Av after midnight one recites Tikkun Rachel alone; during the day one does not recite Tikkun Rachel.
takeaways: On Tisha B'Av one puts on tzitzit and tefillin in the morning at home and recites the Shema, and then goes to the synagogue.
At night after midnight -- Tikkun Rachel alone; during the day one does not recite Tikkun Rachel.

paragraphs: In the Amidah of Ma'ariv and Shacharit, one recites the blessing "Sim Shalom" in its usual manner every day, and one should not shorten it as is printed in the prayer books; and so I instruct the congregation every year. Only the cantor, in the repetition of Shacharit, should say it according to the text written in the prayer books, for I have maintained the custom in the repetition as it was from earlier times. Also, the custom here in our city of Baghdad is to say [the Torah portion] Ha'azinu in place of Shirat HaYam [the Song of the Sea], and in this matter too I have not changed the custom of the congregation; but I myself recite Shirat HaYam as on every other day, and I recite the song of Ha'azinu after the Amidah -- and so do the sages, the God-fearing, and men of [good] deeds.

clarification.explanation: In the Amidah of Ma'ariv and Shacharit one recites the blessing "Sim Shalom" in full as usual, and does not shorten it as printed in the prayer books; only the cantor in the repetition of Shacharit says it according to the printed text. And the custom in Baghdad is to say "Ha'azinu" in place of Shirat HaYam -- Rabbi Yosef Chaim leaves this custom in place for the congregation, but he himself recites Shirat HaYam as usual, and recites Ha'azinu after the Amidah (as do the sages and men of [good] deeds).
takeaways: One recites "Sim Shalom" in full (not shortened), except for the cantor in the repetition of Shacharit.
The Baghdad custom is "Ha'azinu" in place of Shirat HaYam; Rabbi Yosef Chaim recited Shirat HaYam as usual.

paragraphs: A sick person who eats on Tisha B'Av, if his eating was from the time of Minchah Gedolah onward, recites "Nachem" in place of "Retzeh V'hachalitzenu" [in Birkat HaMazon], and says "and may You rebuild Jerusalem, the holy city, speedily in our days; Blessed are You, Hashem, who comforts Zion in the building of Jerusalem." And likewise the text of the concluding blessing in "Nachem" that is recited in the Amidah should conclude thus: "who comforts Zion in the building of Jerusalem," and not as is printed in the prayer books.

clarification.explanation: A sick person who eats on Tisha B'Av, if he ate from the time of Minchah Gedolah onward, recites "Nachem" in place of "Retzeh V'hachalitzenu" in Birkat HaMazon, and concludes "and may You rebuild Jerusalem, the holy city, speedily in our days; Blessed are You, Hashem, who comforts Zion in the building of Jerusalem" (and this is the text of the closing, not as printed in the prayer books). And likewise the concluding text of "Nachem" recited in the Amidah -- one should conclude "who comforts Zion in the building of Jerusalem," not as printed in the prayer books.
takeaways: A sick person who ate on Tisha B'Av (from Minchah Gedolah onward) -- recites "Nachem" in place of "Retzeh" in Birkat HaMazon, concluding "who comforts Zion in the building of Jerusalem."
The concluding text of "Nachem" in the Amidah as well (which everyone recites at Minchah of Tisha B'Av) -- "who comforts Zion in the building of Jerusalem," not as printed in the prayer books.

paragraphs: Some act with extra piety and wash their hands with a complete hand-washing after dark on the night following Tisha B'Av, because during the day they performed only [a partial] hand-washing up to the finger-joints; and so we practice, though this is not an obligation according to the strict letter of the law. And one must be careful to recite the blessing on the [new] moon on the night following Tisha B'Av with joy, and should say in a pleasant voice, with joy of heart: "David, King of Israel, lives and endures."

clarification.explanation: Some act with extra piety and wash their hands with a complete hand-washing after dark on the night following Tisha B'Av (since during the day they washed only up to the finger-joints), and so does Rabbi Yosef Chaim practice, though it is not an obligation according to the law. And one must be careful to recite the blessing on the [new] moon on the night following Tisha B'Av with joy, saying in a pleasant voice and with joy of heart: "David, King of Israel, lives and endures."
takeaways: On the night following Tisha B'Av -- some perform a complete hand-washing (not an obligation).
One recites the blessing on the [new] moon with joy on the night following the fast.
